steps.heading: Functions as Rooms
steps.body:
Think of an executing program like a person walking through a house. Every time a function is called, they enter a new room. They need a temporary workbench to store their local variables while in that room. 

This workbench is the 'Stack Frame'. When the function finishes, the room is destroyed, the workbench is cleared, and the person walks back out into the previous room, picking up exactly where they left off.

steps.heading: The Calling Convention
steps.body:
When a program calls a function, the caller and the callee must agree on how to pass data. This is the Calling Convention. In x64 Linux (System V AMD64 ABI), it's highly optimized: the first six arguments are not placed on the stack. They are passed directly into extremely fast CPU registers.

The order is always: RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9. If a function has more than six arguments, the rest are dumped onto the stack. Memorize this sequence. You cannot exploit 64-bit binaries without knowing it.

steps.heading: Setting up the Room
steps.body: Every function starts with a 'Prologue' to set up its new stack frame, and ends with an 'Epilogue' to tear it down safely.
steps.code:
global _start
section .text

my_function:
    ; --- THE PROLOGUE ---
    ; Save the previous function's base pointer so we don't lose it
    push rbp
    
    ; Set the current stack pointer (RSP) as our new base pointer (RBP)
    ; RBP now securely anchors our new stack frame
    mov rbp, rsp
    
    ; Allocate 32 bytes of space on the stack for our local variables
    ; The stack grows downwards in memory, so we subtract
    sub rsp, 0x20
    
    ; Function logic executes here...
    
    ; --- THE EPILOGUE ---
    ; Restore the stack pointer, effectively deleting our local variables
    mov rsp, rbp
    
    ; Restore the caller's base pointer
    pop rbp
    
    ; Pop the saved return address off the stack and jump to it
    ret

steps.heading: Making the Jump
steps.body: The `call` instruction is actually doing two things at once: it pushes the address of the *next* instruction onto the stack (the return address), and then jumps to the target function.
steps.code:

    ; We want to call a function: calculate(10, 20)
    
    ; Load the first argument into RDI
    mov rdi, 10
    
    ; Load the second argument into RSI
    mov rsi, 20
    
    ; The CALL instruction pushes the address of the next instruction 
    ; (the 'mov rax, 0') onto the top of the stack, then jumps to 'calculate'
    call calculate
    
    ; When 'calculate' finishes and hits 'ret', the CPU pops the return address

steps.heading: The Attacker's Target
steps.body:
Why do security researchers care so much about stack frames? Because of the Return Address.

The return address is literally just a memory pointer sitting on the stack, right next to the function's local variables. If an attacker overflows a local variable, they can rewrite the return address. When the function executes its `ret` instruction, the CPU blindly pops the attacker's fake address off the stack and jumps to it, handing over full control of the program.

steps.heading: The Blind Printer
steps.body:
In C, the `printf` family of functions is magical. You provide a format string with placeholders like `%d` (for integers) or `%s` (for strings), and `printf` replaces them with your variables.

But `printf` is blind. It doesn't actually check how many variables you passed to it. If you give it the format string `%x %x %x`, it blindly assumes there are three variables waiting for it. It will pop three values off the stack or read three registers to fulfill those placeholders, even if you never supplied them.

steps.heading: The Vulnerability
steps.body:
The bug occurs when a lazy programmer passes user input directly into `printf(user_input)` instead of safely isolating it like `printf("%s", user_input)`.

If the attacker inputs the string `%p %p %p`, the vulnerable program will interpret the attacker's input as formatting instructions. Instead of printing the literal text '%p', `printf` starts aggressively leaking memory pointers straight off the execution stack, exposing base addresses, stack canaries, and passwords.

steps.heading: From Read to Write
steps.body:
Information disclosure is bad, but Format Strings can also achieve Remote Code Execution. This is due to a dark, forgotten format specifier: `%n`.

While `%d` and `%s` read data, `%n` WRITES data. Specifically, it counts the number of characters `printf` has outputted so far, and writes that integer into a memory address provided on the stack. By padding our output with spaces (e.g., `%100x`), we can manipulate that character count and write arbitrary values into memory, overwriting function pointers to hijack control flow.

steps.heading: The Death of the Stack
steps.body:
Years ago, attackers could simply inject raw assembly code (shellcode) into a buffer and jump to it. Modern operating systems killed this with NX (No-Execute) / DEP (Data Execution Prevention). The OS marks the stack as 'read/write, but never execute'.

If the CPU tries to run instructions located on the stack, it triggers a hardware exception and the program instantly dies. To survive, attackers had to adapt. If they can't bring their own weapons, they have to use the weapons already lying around the room.

steps.heading: Frankenstein's Exploit
steps.body:
Return Oriented Programming (ROP) bypasses NX by chaining together tiny snippets of executable code that already exist in the binary or system libraries (like `libc`). These snippets are called 'Gadgets'.

A gadget is typically 2-3 instructions ending in a `ret` (return) instruction. The attacker overflows the stack not with shellcode, but with a carefully ordered list of memory addresses pointing to these gadgets. The CPU executes a gadget, hits the `ret`, pops the next address off the attacker's stack, and jumps to the next gadget.

steps.heading: The Stack Pivot
steps.body:
Sometimes, the buffer you overflow is too small to hold a massive 20-gadget ROP chain. In these scenarios, you perform a 'Stack Pivot'.

You place your full ROP chain in a larger memory area (like the heap or a global variable). Then, you use your limited stack overflow to execute a single gadget like `pop rsp; ret` or `xchg rsp, rax; ret`. This forcefully rips the stack pointer away from its normal location and points it directly at your massive secondary payload. The CPU blindly continues executing the chain from the new location.

steps.heading: The Anti-Magic Language
steps.body:
Go (Golang) was built by Google to solve massive backend scaling problems. Its philosophy is brutal simplicity. There is no inheritance, no classes, no try/catch exceptions, and absolutely no hidden magic.

If C is a racecar that occasionally explodes, and Python is a comfortable minivan, Go is a bullet train. It is strongly typed, compiles instantly to a static binary, and has built-in concurrency primitives. For malware developers and red teamers, Go's ability to cross-compile self-contained binaries for Windows, Linux, and macOS simultaneously makes it the ultimate weaponization tool.

steps.heading: Variables and Speed
steps.body:
Go is statically typed, but you rarely have to write the types. The short variable declaration `:=` infers the type automatically, making it feel as fast as writing Python while keeping the strict safety of C++.

Go also enforces cleanliness at the compiler level. If you declare a variable or import a package and don't use it, your code will refuse to compile. It forces you to write lean, garbage-free code.

steps.heading: The Defer Keyword
steps.body:
Memory leaks and dangling file handles are common bugs. Go solves this beautifully with the `defer` keyword.

When you `defer` a function call, it pushes that execution onto a stack. The deferred function is guaranteed to run right before the surrounding function finishes, regardless of whether it returned naturally or panicked. It allows you to place your setup and teardown code immediately next to each other, so you never forget to close a socket or release a lock.

steps.heading: Networking Made Native
steps.body:
Writing a TCP server in C involves a nightmare of struct definitions, byte-order conversions, `socket()`, `bind()`, `listen()`, and `accept()`. 

Go abstracts all of this into the standard library's `net` package. Network streams in Go implement the exact same `Reader` and `Writer` interfaces as local files. This means code written to read data from a text file can instantly read data from a remote TCP socket with zero modifications. It is powerfully elegant.

steps.heading: Listeners and Dialers
steps.body:
In Go networking, the paradigm is simple. Servers use `net.Listen` to open a port and wait for connections. Clients use `net.Dial` to reach out and connect to a listening port.

Once a connection is established, both sides receive a `net.Conn` object. You treat this object exactly like a two-way pipe: you write bytes into it to send data, and you read bytes out of it to receive data.

steps.heading: Effortless Concurrency
steps.body:
A server that can only handle one client at a time is useless. In older languages, handling multiple clients requires complex multi-threading or async event loops. 

Go uses 'goroutines'. A goroutine is a lightweight virtual thread managed by the Go runtime. By simply putting the word `go` in front of a function call, Go rips that function execution off the main thread and runs it concurrently in the background. A Go server can easily spin up 10,000 goroutines to handle 10,000 concurrent network connections without breaking a sweat.
